content:
Paul is often presented as a convert who brought the gospel of Jesus to the nations, and his earlier life as a short prelude. The early life matters more than that. His letters are the oldest Christian writings that survive, and his authority rests on a vision he received after Jesus had gone, so who he was before the vision bears on everything after it.

Two kinds of source describe him. His own letters say a little, and the Book of Acts, written later by an admirer, says more. The difference between them needs to be kept in view at every step.

This article aims to provide context to Paul's life before the Damascus road, insha'Allah, in six facts, each marked by the source that gives it. The Quran names no Paul; it names the disciples of Jesus as "Allah's helpers" (61:14), and the question is how Paul stands beside them.[1]

Paul describes himself in his own words: "circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; concerning the law, a Pharisee" (Philippians 3:5). He says it again in Romans: "I also am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin" (Romans 11:1).[2]

These come from letters that scholars of every school accept as his own. His later arguments about the Law of Moses were made by a man who had kept it, and who says he had been "blameless" in its righteousness (Philippians 3:6).[2]

"I am indeed a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel" (Acts 22:3).[3] Tarsus, in the south of modern Turkey, was a Greek-speaking city of the Roman province of Cilicia.

Paul's own letters never name Tarsus. He says only that after his conversion he "came to the regions of Syria and Cilicia" (Galatians 1:21), which fits Acts without proving it.[2] Claims that Tarsus schooled him in Greek philosophy or mystery religions go beyond the evidence: a city's culture shows what he could have met, and nothing about what he took from it.

A popular telling has Saul renamed Paul at his conversion. Acts tells it differently. The conversion comes in chapter 9, and the name Paul first appears four chapters later, with no renaming at all: "Saul, who is also called Paul" (Acts 13:9).[3]

Saul is the Hebrew name of the first king of Israel, a Benjaminite like Paul. Paulus is a Roman family name. A Jew of the Roman world could carry both, and every letter under his name uses the Roman one.

Paul calls himself a Pharisee (Philippians 3:5), and writes that he "advanced in the Jews' religion beyond many of my own age", being "more exceedingly zealous for the traditions of my fathers" (Galatians 1:14).[2]

Acts adds that he studied under Gamaliel in Jerusalem (Acts 22:3), the same Gamaliel whom Acts presents in the council as "a teacher of the law, honored by all the people", urging restraint towards the apostles (Acts 5:34).[3] Paul's letters do not mention Gamaliel, so the detail rests on Acts alone. His command of scripture in his letters is plain either way.

In Jerusalem, about to be flogged, Paul claims Roman citizenship. The commander says, "I bought my citizenship for a great price," and Paul answers, "But I was born a Roman" (Acts 22:27 to 28).[3] Citizenship protected him from punishment without trial, and Acts later has him appeal to Caesar on the strength of it.

Paul's letters never mention his citizenship. How his family gained it is unknown, and any account of his parents or their wealth is invention.

On this point Paul and Acts agree. "Beyond measure I persecuted the assembly of God, and ravaged it" (Galatians 1:13); he counts himself "the least of the apostles, who is not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God" (1 Corinthians 15:9).[2] Acts places him at the stoning of Stephen: "Saul was consenting to his death" (Acts 8:1).[3]

The record shows a zealous opponent of the movement who later claimed to lead its mission to the Gentiles. It does not show a secret plan to subvert it from within, and Muslims should not claim what the record does not show. Apostle of Doom examines his record as Saul the persecutor. We set out how Paul's claim to be an apostle was received by those who had known Jesus in Paul's claim to apostleship.

The bottom line

Paul's own letters establish that he was a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin, a Pharisee zealous for the traditions of his fathers, and a persecutor of the followers of Jesus. Acts adds his birth in Tarsus, his teacher Gamaliel and his Roman citizenship, none of which his letters confirm. Saul and Paul were two names he carried at once.

None of this makes him one of the disciples whom the Quran honours. They walked with Jesus, and Paul did not; his authority rests on what he says he saw later. The Quran's measure of every claim about Jesus stays the same: "Christ Jesus the son of Mary was (no more than) a messenger of Allah" (4:171).[1] Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Quran 4:171; 61:14, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  2. Philippians 3:5 to 6; Romans 11:1; Galatians 1:13 to 21; 1 Corinthians 15:9 (World English Bible).
  3. Acts 5:34; 8:1; 13:9; 22:3; 22:27 to 28 (World English Bible).
